q: In physics, work is done only when an object moves under the influence of a force.
e: True. In physics, work is done only when an object moves under the influence of a force. Work needs a force and a displacement along that force. No movement, no work.

q: Work may be defined as the scalar product of the force applied and the displacement.
e: True. Work may be defined as the scalar product of the force applied and the displacement. Dot products make scalars with cos θ. Cross products make perpendicular vectors with sin θ.

q: The work by a force is given by the equation $W = Fs \cos \theta$.
e: True. The work by a force is given by the equation W = Fs cos θ. Work is W = Fs cos θ, the scalar product of force and displacement.

q: The change in potential energy is equal to the work done on the object.
e: True. The change in potential energy is equal to the work done on the object. The change of potential energy equals the work done against the conservative force.

q: The rate of doing work is defined as power.
e: True. The rate of doing work is defined as power. Power is work per unit time. In SI that unit is the watt: 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.

q: The unit for power in SI units is the watt (W).
e: True. The unit for power in SI units is the watt (W). SI power is the watt. Erg per second is CGS.

q: If the work done is 1 joule in 1 second, the power is 1 watt.
e: True. If the work done is 1 joule in 1 second, the power is 1 watt. One joule in one second is one watt.

q: The units of power which are larger than watt are kilowatt (kW) and megawatt (MW).
e: True. The units of power which are larger than watt are kilowatt (kW) and megawatt (MW). 1 kW = 10³ W and 1 MW = 10⁶ W.

q: $1 \text{ kW} = 1000 \text{ W} = 10^3 \text{ W}$.
e: True. 1 kW = 1000 W = 10³ W. 1 kW = 10³ W and 1 MW = 10⁶ W.
True. 1 MW = 1000000 W = 10^6 W. 1 kW = 10³ W and 1 MW = 10⁶ W.

q: In the CGS system, the unit of power is erg s$^{-1}$.
e: True. In the CGS system, the unit of power is erg s^-1. CGS power is the erg per second.

q: In the British system, the unit of power is foot-pound per second (ft-lb s$^{-1}$).
e: True. In the British system, the unit of power is foot-pound per second (ft-lb s^-1). 550 ft-lb in one second is one horsepower.

q: In the British engineering system, the unit of power is horse power (hp).
e: True. In the British engineering system, the unit of power is horse power (hp). Horsepower is the British engineering unit of power.

q: If the work done in 1 second is 550 ft-lb, the power is 1 horse power.
e: True. If the work done in 1 second is 550 ft-lb, the power is 1 horse power. Horsepower is the British engineering unit of power.
True. 1 W = 1 J s^-1 = 10^7 erg s^-1. CGS power is the erg per second.

q: $1 \text{ hp} = 550 \text{ ft-lb s}^{-1} = 746 \text{ W}$.
e: True. 1 hp = 550 ft-lb s^-1 = 746 W. 1 kW = 1000 W, 1 MW = 10⁶ W, and 1 hp = 746 W = 550 ft-lb s⁻¹.

q: Power is equal to the product of force and velocity ($P = Fv$).
e: True. Power is equal to the product of force and velocity (P = Fv). At constant speed, power is force times velocity, P = Fv.

q: Power is a fundamental concept of physics.
e: False. The fundamental is the lowest standing-wave frequency. Higher ones are harmonics or overtones.

q: Car engines, water pumps, refrigerators, air conditioners and electric bulbs are specified according to their power consumption.
e: True. Car engines, water pumps, refrigerators, air conditioners and electric bulbs are specified according to their power consumption. Machines are rated by the power they consume or deliver.

q: $1 \text{ kW} = 10^6 \text{ W}$.
e: False. 1 kW = 10³ W and 1 MW = 10⁶ W.

q: $1 \text{ hp} = 750 \text{ W}$.
e: False. 1 kW = 1000 W, 1 MW = 10⁶ W, and 1 hp = 746 W = 550 ft-lb s⁻¹.

q: In the British system, the unit of power is the joule per second.
e: False. In the British system, the unit of power is foot-pound per second (ft-lb s^-1). Work is F · s. Power is work per second, in watts.

q: Power is equal to the product of mass and velocity.
e: False. The claim puts mass where force belongs. Power is equal to the product of force and velocity (P = Fv). Work is F · s.

q: The rate of energy change is also important in practice.
e: True. The rate of energy change is also important in practice. rate has to stay in that role in the sentence.

q: If $s$ is the displacement produced by a constant force $F$ acting for the time $t$, the work done is $Fs$.
e: True. If s is the displacement produced by a constant force F acting for the time t, the work done is Fs. Work is F · s. Power is work per second, in watts.

q: For uniform motion, velocity $v$ is constant, so $P = Fv$.
e: True. For uniform motion, velocity v is constant, so P = Fv. At constant speed, power is force times velocity, P = Fv.

q: In the CGS system, if the work done is 1 erg in 1 second, the power is 1 erg s$^{-1}$.
e: True. In the CGS system, if the work done is 1 erg in 1 second, the power is 1 erg s^-1. CGS power is the erg per second.

q: $1 \text{ hp} = 746 \times 10^7 \text{ erg s}^{-1}$.
e: True. 1 hp = 746 × 10^7 erg s^-1. CGS power is the erg per second.
